title: Bounded Loads
description: Explore Google's bounded-load consistent hashing algorithm, power of two choices, load factor epsilon, and real implementation in Envoy proxy.

segments.text: Consistent hashing solves the rehashing problem beautifully. But it has a dirty secret: load distribution can be terribly uneven. With a hundred keys and five nodes, you might see one node holding forty percent of the keys while another holds five percent. Virtual nodes help, but Google found a better fix.

In 2016, Google published a paper on consistent hashing with bounded loads. The core insight: even with virtual nodes, hash functions create statistical imbalance. In production, they observed some servers receiving two to three times the average load. At Google's scale, that means some servers are on fire while others idle.

The algorithm adds one rule: no node can exceed one plus epsilon times the average load. Epsilon is your tuning knob. Set epsilon to zero point two five, and no node exceeds one hundred twenty-five percent of the average. When a request maps to an overloaded node, it walks clockwise to the next node that has capacity.

Epsilon controls the trade-off between balance and consistency. Low epsilon like zero point one means near-perfect balance, but more keys get displaced from their natural home. High epsilon like one point zero means better cache hit rates but more imbalance. Google found zero point two five to be the sweet spot for most workloads.
segments.thought_prompt: If you set epsilon to zero, what would happen? Would it even work?

segments.text: A related technique is the power of two choices. Instead of hashing to one node, hash to two random nodes and pick the less loaded one. This sounds almost too simple, but the math is remarkable. It reduces max load from O of log n over log log n to O of log log n. An exponential improvement from just one extra choice.

Google's bounded-load algorithm combines both ideas. Hash to the ring to find the primary node. If it's overloaded, check the next node clockwise. This preserves consistent hashing's property that most keys stay put when nodes change, while guaranteeing bounded imbalance. Best of both worlds.

Envoy proxy implements this as its ring hash load balancer with bounded loads. In the config, you set the hash policy for consistent routing and a max ring size. When a backend exceeds the load factor, Envoy spills traffic to the next host on the ring. Istio service meshes use this in production at massive scale.

The catch: you need global state. Every proxy must know the current load on every node to enforce the bound. In a single proxy, that's trivial. In a fleet of a thousand Envoy sidecars, you either accept approximate counts or centralize load tracking. Most production deployments use local approximate counting, which works surprisingly well.
segments.thought_prompt: If each proxy has slightly stale load information, could the bounded guarantee be violated?

segments.text: Use bounded loads when you have stateful routing requirements like sticky sessions or caching, but can't tolerate hot spots. Classic use case: a CDN cache cluster where you want consistent hashing for cache hits but can't afford one server melting. Vimeo uses this exact pattern for their video cache tier.

Bounded loads is what makes consistent hashing production-ready at scale. Without it, you're hoping your hash function distributes evenly. With it, you're guaranteeing it. And in distributed systems, hope is not a strategy.
